old: Long before it held your coats, this word named a fenced-in patch of open ground, not a room at all.
Its French ancestor meant a small, private, walled-off space — but out under the sky, not inside a house.
It's built the same way as the word close plus a diminutive ending — literally, a 'little shut-off place.'
clues: This small household space began in French as a word only for little open-air enclosures, a fenced-off patch of outdoor ground rather than any kind of room.
Built into the wall rather than freestanding like a wardrobe, it's a small enclosed space with a door, often holding hanging clothes. English first used it for small private rooms.
Families keep skeletons in one, and people come out of one when they reveal they're gay. It shares its root with close, from Latin meaning shut or enclosed.
